prerequisites: Good knowledge of real and complex calculus
Good knowledge of functional analysis (representation and operations with real and complex variable functions)

learning_outcomes.text: Students will have demonstrated possession and understanding of knowledge in a field of study that builds on general secondary education, and is typically at a level that, although supported by advanced textbooks, also includes aspects involving knowledge from the forefront of their field of study.

Students will be able to apply their knowledge to their work or vocation in a professional manner and possess the competencies typically demonstrated by developing and defending arguments and solving problems within their field of study.
Students will have the ability to gather and interpret relevant data (usually within their field of study) to make judgments that include reflection on relevant social, scientific, or ethical issues.
Students will be able to transmit information, ideas, problems, and solutions to both specialized and non-specialized audiences.
Students will have developed the learning skills necessary to undertake further studies with a high degree of autonomy.

Choose and apply the most appropriate methods and techniques to analyze and solve problems defined by data that pose a challenge due to their volume, velocity, variety, or heterogeneity, including computational, mathematical, statistical, and signal processing methods.

Possess the experimental and analytical skills to work autonomously, being able to design experiments and describe, analyze, evaluate, and interpret the resulting information to propose alternative and novel solutions to known and/or emerging problems.
Create models and make decisions based on available data, combining acquired knowledge and being able to apply new knowledge to problem-solving.
Ability to integrate into a multidisciplinary team within the framework of a data science project.
Ability to access and manage information in different formats for subsequent analysis to obtain knowledge from data.
Ability to express the results of data processing clearly and convincingly both in writing and orally.
Understanding and mastery of the basic concepts of information, signal, and system theory, used in different schemes and techniques for data representation and manipulation.
Ability to analyze, encode, process, and transmit information and data using signal processing techniques.
Know how to represent a signal from samples and reconstruct a signal from its samples.
Know how to characterize signals and data in different domains (time, frequency, spatial, etc.), and know how to transform between these domains.
Ability to evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of different implementation alternatives for information processing systems, from the perspective of signal space, disturbances, and noise.
Ability to have a global vision of a complex signal and data processing system and the interactions between its components.

Understand the concept of analog and digital signals and data. Manage sampling, interpolation, quantization operations, and associated theorems and transformations (Fourier series expansion, Fourier transform, Laplace transform, and Z-transform).
Know how to apply signals and systems concepts to solve dimensionality reduction problems in datasets.
Know how to apply signals and systems concepts to select the most suitable space for data treatment, as well as to represent and operate with data in that space.

syllabus_topics: Relationship between algebra/calculus and signal and system theory
Review of vector spaces and particularization of signal spaces
Definition of the Dirac delta and physical meaning
Relationship of the Dirac delta with the step function
Operations with distributions (derivatives, convolutions, product and system resolution)
Relationship of FSE with linear and invariant systems
Relationship between the FT and linear and invariant systems
Periodic signals: Fourier series expansion (FSE) of discrete signals
Definition of the FSE for discrete variable signals
Convergence of the FSE for discrete variable signals
Properties of the FSE for discrete variable signals
Examples of the FSE for discrete variable signals
Relationship of FSE with linear and invariant systems
Aperiodic signals: Fourier transform (FT) of discrete signals
Definition of the FT for discrete variable signals
Convergence of the FT for discrete variable signals
Properties of the FT for discrete variable signals
Examples of the FT for discrete variable signals
Relationship of the FT with linear and invariant systems
Signals and systems of continuous and discrete variables
Sampling and recovery of continuous variable signals
Modeling of a continuous LTI system using a discrete LTI system
teaching_methods: Presential activities: expository classes (chalkboard, transparencies, audiovisuals)
Asynchronous non-presential activities (flexible and autonomous student work)
Documentary material and/or audiovisual content or simulation tools for non-presential activities
Doubt resolution via telematic means (email, virtual campus platforms)
Doubt resolution via face-to-face activities (during classes or office hours)
Collaboration among students for doubt resolution

assessment_methods.method: Active participation in forums and virtual campus activities [CV]

assessment_rules: For the ordinary call, the final grade is calculated as: Final Grade = PS * 0.05 + CV * D * 0.1 + ET * 0.4 + EP * 0.45, where PS, CV, ET, and EP are on a scale of 0 to 10, and D is binary (0 or 1). Grades obtained in the ordinary call are not valid for any other call. For extraordinary calls, the final grade is calculated as: Final Grade = ET * 0.5 + EP * 0.5. Students with a recognized differentiated evaluation system will be assessed according to the extraordinary call system.
